extracted.intended_audience: educational institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, and legal counsel implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for educational institutions (K-12 and postsecondary) to design and carry out Title IX grievance processes, including parties' rights to discuss allegations, gather evidence, select advisors, receive written notice, and protections against retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.45(b)(5)(iii) — Recipients must not restrict parties' ability to discuss allegations under investigation or to gather and present evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: This provision contains two related requirements: that a recipient not restrict a party's ability (i) to discuss the allegations under investigation and (ii) to gather and present evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains both purposes: (i) permitting parties to speak or write about the allegations (e.g., to parents, friends, advocacy organizations) so they can seek emotional support, advice, or engage in public discussion about institutional policies; and (ii) permitting parties to contact potential witnesses, inspect locations, take photographs, or otherwise collect evidence to meaningfully participate in advancing their interests. The provision's two requirements sometimes overlap (e.g., discussing allegations to identify witnesses). It is limited in scope to discussion of "the allegations under investigation," and does not cover evidence exchanged under §106.45(b)(5)(vi) or the investigative report under §106.45(b)(5)(vii). Abusive speech (defamation, privacy torts) and unlawful retaliation remain prohibited; such abuses can be addressed by tort law and §106.71.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation — applies only when a formal complaint is filed and only to 'the allegations under investigation'
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5)(iii) applies only where allegations are made in a formal complaint; it does not apply to a mere report of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the provision applies only once a formal complaint is filed, recipients retain discretion to impose non-disclosure or confidentiality requirements on complainants and respondents prior to a formal complaint. Also, the provision's protection does not extend to evidence subject to inspection and review under §106.45(b)(5)(vi) or to investigative reports under §106.45(b)(5)(vii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses of discussion and other misconduct remain prohibited (retaliation, defamation, torts, witness tampering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties' right to discuss allegations or contact witnesses is not a blanket immunity for unlawful conduct: defamation, invasion of privacy, retaliation, witness tampering, intimidation, or other interference remain prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations add §106.71 prohibiting retaliation ("No recipient or other person may intimidate, threaten, coerce, or discriminate against any individual for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by title IX or this part"). Conduct that constitutes tampering (e.g., attempting to alter or prevent witness testimony) is also prohibited under §106.71(a). Inconsistencies arising from a party speaking with a witness are to be weighed by investigators/decision-makers and do not automatically constitute interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients should not impose prior restraints on parties' expressive activities about allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should not, under the guise of confidentiality, impose prior restraints on a student's or employee's ability to speak or write about allegations under investigation (for example, with parents, friends, or advocacy organizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department observed that restricting such discussion can isolate parties and chill participation; student activism and publication about Title IX procedures can be important for institutional reform. However, the right is limited to discussing the allegations under investigation and does not immunize tortious or retaliatory speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must permit parties to gather and present evidence to ensure equal opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must not hamper a party's ability to collect evidence relevant to the case (e.g., contacting witnesses, photographing locations) so that parties have equal opportunity to advance their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement makes other procedural rights meaningful (for example, the right to inspect and review evidence). If a party is prevented from gathering evidence, the investigatory and adjudicatory process may be impaired; missing or destroyed evidence can be addressed and weighed in determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.45(b)(5)(iv) — Advisors of Choice: parties' right to select and have advisors present
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide all parties the same opportunities to have advisors present and to have advisors participate in Title IX proceedings, subject to equal restrictions on advisors' participation in the recipient's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations clarify that a party's advisor may be, but is not required to be, an attorney, and that recipients may not limit the choice or presence of an advisor. Allowing advisors promotes a fairer, more thorough process. Recipients retain discretion to place equal limits on advisors' active participation (e.g., requiring parties personally to answer certain questions), but such rules must apply equally to both parties. For postsecondary institutions, when live hearings are held, the advisor must conduct cross-examination on behalf of the party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisors' status (attorney or non-attorney) and parties' financial resources must not affect compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that an advisor is an attorney, or that a party has greater financial means to obtain counsel, must not affect the recipient's compliance with Title IX procedural requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations do not require recipients to provide or pay for advisors, but they may choose to do so. The recipient must treat parties equally regardless of advisor status or party finances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may require advisors to maintain confidentiality consistent with FERPA and may use NDAs consistent with the regulations and other laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may require advisors to use evidence received under inspection and review and investigative reports only for the grievance process and to refrain from further dissemination or disclosure; recipients may use non-disclosure agreements that comply with the final regulations and other applicable laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations are to be interpreted consistent with a recipient's FERPA obligations (§106.6(e)). Recipients can lawfully limit dissemination of confidential materials by advisors provided such limits comply with Title IX and other laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest rule for Title IX personnel does not apply to party advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: The §106.45(b)(1)(iii) prohibition on Title IX personnel having conflicts of interest or bias does not apply to party advisors (including institution-provided advisors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisors may also be witnesses; potential conflicts involving advisors serving as witnesses do not violate the regulations but may affect the weight and credibility of their testimony. Recipients retain discretion to evaluate credibility accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may place equal restrictions on advisors' active participation
rubrics_metrics.description: While parties have a right to advisors of choice, recipients may adopt and enforce reasonable restrictions on advisors' active participation so long as any such restrictions apply equally to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to specify exhaustive permissible restrictions; examples include requiring parties personally to answer investigator questions or to make opening/closing statements. Recipients should ensure restrictions do not create unequal procedural advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: For postsecondary live hearings, cross-examination must be conducted by a party's advisor on the party's behalf
rubrics_metrics.description: When live hearings are held by postsecondary institutions, the recipient must permit a party's advisor to conduct cross-examination on behalf of the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement need not be more extensive than permitting the advisor to relay the party's desired questions to other parties and witnesses. This approach distinguishes the advisor role in Title IX proceedings from criminal counsel and preserves recipients' discretion over advisor participation rules applied equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.45(b)(5)(v) — Written notice of hearings, meetings, and investigative interviews with sufficient time to prepare
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide written notice to a party of the date, time, location, participants, and nature of interviews, meetings, and hearings where the party's participation is invited or expected, and provide sufficient time to prepare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written notice promotes fairness and due process, helps parties prepare (including seeking accommodations), and reduces misunderstandings compared to oral notice. Nothing prevents recipients from also giving notice by other means (in-person, phone), and written notice helps track rescheduling. The provision is intended to apply only to the party whose participation is invited or expected. Copies of evidence subject to inspection and the investigative report must be provided to parties and their advisors (electronically or in hard copy). The initial written notice must include a statement about whether the recipient's code of conduct prohibits false statements (§106.45(b)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients should not limit parties' discussion to 'neutral' communications or only for gathering evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department rejects suggestions that discussions be limited only to neutral communications or communications solely for gathering witnesses/evidence, because such limits would deprive parties of emotional support and expressive purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting communications to neutral or evidence-gathering purposes would prevent parties from seeking emotional support or publicly discussing perceived flaws in policies. Recipients retain other tools (retaliation prohibition, tort remedies, no-contact orders) to address harmful communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may issue mutual no-contact orders and other supportive measures consistent with §106.30
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain discretion to restrict parties' contact or communication with each other (e.g., mutual no-contact orders) as supportive measures under §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures are distinct from restrictions on a party's broader ability to discuss allegations or gather evidence and may be employed to protect parties during investigation and adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients should not unilaterally decide who has a 'need to know' or label information confidential to restrict discussion of allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department believes parties, not recipients, should determine who has a legitimate need to know about the allegations in order to provide advice, support, or assistance during the grievance process; recipients should not label information "confidential" to impede parties' discussions of allegations under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting recipients to control 'need to know' or confidentiality labeling would undermine parties' ability to seek support. Recipients may, however, lawfully impose limitations on the dissemination of evidence per inspection/review rules and FERPA where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence access and inspection — parties must be given equal opportunity to inspect and review evidence gathered by the recipient under §106.45(b)(5)(vi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although discussed in connection with notice and other provisions, the final regulations require that both parties have equal opportunity to inspect and review all evidence gathered by the recipient that is directly related to the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing adequate notice and evidence copies to parties (and their advisors) ensures fairness and makes the right to inspect evidence meaningful; if evidence appears missing or destroyed, parties and decision-makers may address that in assessing credibility and the weight of evidence.
